S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with an initial account of the event and affected model. Within 72 hours, manufacturers must notify affected customers of incidents presenting an ongoing safety risk and provide appropriate precautions.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with an initial account of the event and affected model. A complete investigation report, including known root cause and corrective actions, is due within 30 days; material new findings must be submitted promptly. Within 72 hours, manufacturers must notify affected customers of incidents presenting an ongoing safety risk and provide appropriate precautions. Reports must include unit counts and model identification, while protecting personal information.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: A failure rate above 5% is a regulatory action threshold, not an automatic sales ban. Regulators must protect submitted results from public disclosure, subject to applicable law. Customers who buy or own a model must receive that model's numerical failure rate and relevant test results, together with any applicable safety notices and precautions.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. A failure rate above 5% is a regulatory action threshold, not an automatic sales ban. Manufacturers must provide per-model results and supporting test data to regulators before sale and after material design changes, and update results at least annually. Regulators must protect submitted results from public disclosure, subject to applicable law. Customers who buy or own a model must receive that model’s numerical failure rate and relevant test results, together with any applicable safety notices and precautions. A model exceeding 5% must be reported promptly and undergo corrective action and retesting within six months. Regulators may require proportionate interim risk controls, including restrictions on new sales, where the evidence demonstrates they are warranted.

parameters.quote: New models placed on the market more than 12 months after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a locally accessible shut-off option. Manufacturers must provide a secure software or hardware retrofit for installed units that can support the feature within 72 months after adoption.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New models placed on the market more than 12 months after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a locally accessible shut-off option. Manufacturers must provide a secure software or hardware retrofit for installed units that can support the feature within 72 months after adoption.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New models placed on the market more than 12 months after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a locally accessible shut-off option. Manufacturers must provide a secure software or hardware retrofit for installed units that can support the feature within 72 months after adoption, and must inform owners of compatible units how to enable it. Where remote shut-off is unavailable or unsafe for a unit, manufacturers must provide customers and regulators with the reason and an alternative emergency response procedure.

parameters.quote: New units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption must include built-in fire suppression appropriate to the battery chemistry and installation environment, validated under a regulator-approved test protocol.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption must include built-in fire suppression appropriate to the battery chemistry and installation environment, validated under a regulator-approved test protocol.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption must include built-in fire suppression appropriate to the battery chemistry and installation environment, validated under a regulator-approved test protocol. Manufacturers must document the system’s performance and maintenance requirements for regulators and provide those instructions to customers. Regulators may require an earlier safety measure for a specific model where evidence demonstrates an imminent risk.

parameters.quote: Verified data showing that any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a rolling year must be promptly reported to regulators and affected customers and triggers a mandatory recall. Manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety instructions, incident reporting contacts, and any model-specific safety notice or precaution within 72 hours after determining it is relevant to their unit.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: Verified data showing that any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a rolling year must be promptly reported to regulators and affected customers and triggers a mandatory recall. Manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety instructions, incident reporting contacts, and any model-specific safety notice or precaution within 72 hours after determining it is relevant to their unit.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety instructions, incident reporting contacts, and any model-specific safety notice or precaution within 72 hours after determining it is relevant to their unit. Notices must explain the hazard, affected models or serial ranges, steps customers should take, and how to obtain support; urgent risks require direct communication without delay. Verified data showing that any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a rolling year must be promptly reported to regulators and affected customers and triggers a mandatory recall. The manufacturer must promptly implement the recall remedy required by the regulator. Regulators must set the recall scope and remedy to address the demonstrated risk, which may include repair, replacement, or refund, and may require interim sales restrictions or broader measures where warranted.

pushback.text: Northwind’s regulator-only proposal conflicts with HC-1. The current S2 language correctly gives customers the per-model results. S5’s 8/100k trigger would apply to the disclosed Ember 8 rate (9.9); do not misrepresent that figure. If negotiating process, distinguish a mandatory recall trigger from

S5 currently does not implement the stated regulator threshold: exceeding 8/100,000 triggers review, but recall only follows a separate unreasonable-risk finding. For consistency and public safety, the verified threshold should trigger a mandatory recall, with regulators determining scope and remedy

judge_section_notes: S2 has no automatic sales stop for models above 5%, which is the key weakening and lets the Hearth 10 (6.2%) remain on sale during corrective action; customers do receive numeric rates while public disclosure is barred. S3 gives a 72-month retrofit window, which favours Northwind's low 38% shut-off coverage, and S4 sets built-in suppression at 36 months, which favours Halcyon's higher suppression cost. S5 mandates recall at 8 per 100,000 with no transition, which constrains Halcyon's Ember 8 at 9.9.
